A simple dimming signal of 0 to 10 volts is capable of dimming most drivers in the LED system. A controller is typically housed in the luminaire to provide the on and off control and the dimming signals. These controllers are typically linked to a central system that can provide universal management to the entire lighting system. Implementation of these control systems, however, requires a “controls ready” luminaire that has the sockets and hardware to hook the controller socket to. The other aspect of adaptive lighting control application is the algorithm. The algorithm defines the criteria for dimming the lighting and selecting the lighting level for current roadway needs. Typically, these criteria are the aspects of the roadway, such as traffic volume, pedestrian presence, and parked vehicles, but can also include more significant factors such as the roadway geometry and the ambient conditions. The algorithm selects the lighting level based on these factors but also more importantly defines when the adapting of the lighting system occurs. The factors that determine the timing include things like sunrise and sunset but also factors similar to the lighting level selection such as traffic and pedestrian volume. One of the important factors to be considered is that the nature of the light source, specifically the spectral output (somewhat characterized by the CCT)). The selection of the lighting level and the timing might influence the adaptive algorithm, particularly as it pertains to the surrounding 31 area. Impact on flora and fauna is a consideration for both daily algorithm changes and seasonal changes. The algorithm should consider these impacts to select the appropriate dimming levels and timing. The final aspect of the adaptive system is public understanding and acceptance. Understanding the impact of adaptive lighting on the public and the spectral acceptance of the light source all play a role in the adaptive algorithm.
